entries.name: Perry, written on the base
entries.looks_like: The name Perry written by hand on the base of a small early piece.
entries.means: Made by Mary Chase Perry in her first workshop, before the pottery had a settled name.
entries.date_note: Her first years of pottery, about 1900 to 1903, before the Pewabic name (dated 1903 by Pewabic and Catallo, 1905 in one passage of Pear). Pewabic and Catallo say she signed in ink or glaze; Pear's photograph does not show which.

entries.name: MCP, her initials
entries.looks_like: The capital letters M C P on the base, pressed into the clay, scratched in, or written.
entries.means: Mary Chase Perry's initials, her own mark on early work.
entries.date_note: Barber printed it as in use in 1904. No source gives a first or last year; about 1901 to 1907 are the years of her first workshop. Barber says impressed; Pewabic and Catallo say written in ink or glaze; a Minneapolis vase has it scratched in. All three seem to exist.

sources.where: p. 229, as given in Lehner (1988), Lehner p. 342

disagreements: Barber says the initials are impressed; Catallo and the Pewabic timeline say 'hand-signed' MCP in ink or glaze; the Minneapolis Institute of Art records MCP incised. Probably all three exist.

entries.name: Revelation Pottery triangle
entries.looks_like: A triangle with REVELATION up the left side and POTTERY down the right, a candle in a holder inside, M.C.P. under it and DETROIT along the bottom.
entries.means: Fired in Horace Caulkins's Revelation kilns, before the name Pewabic; Revelation was the kiln's brand. Pear calls it her earliest and rarest seal.
entries.date_note: Brunk dates the first pieces to the Revelation kiln's introduction in April 1901 and shows examples of about 1904; the Detroit Institute of Arts dates its example about 1905; Evans says it was used only for a year before 1906.

sources.where: p. 229, as given in Lehner (1988), Lehner p. 342 and mark no. 6, p. 343

disagreements: Years: Brunk 2007 - from April 1901 (kiln demonstration pieces); Pear - the first Stable-Studio years, before the Pewabic name (which Pear dates 1905); Evans (as Lehner gives him) - only for a year before 1906; the Detroit Institute of Arts dates its example about 1905; Brunk's examples 1904 and about 1904.
What is inside the triangle: the Detroit Institute of Arts and Lehner's drawing - a candle in a holder; Pear - 'the flame'. Probably the same device (the kiln flame drawn as a candle).

Catallo (p. 34) mentions 'a paper label with a triangular "Pewabic Pottery Detroit"' as a later mark; no other source describes a triangular Pewabic label, and no example was found. It may be a confusion with this Revelation triangle.

entries.name: Five leaves over PEWABIC
entries.looks_like: A row of five small leaves in an arc with PEWABIC curving underneath, pressed into the clay. Museums also call it the crescent mark, or PEWABIC under five flames.
entries.means: Pewabic's first standard mark, on the matte-glazed ware of the first workshop.
entries.date_note: 1903 to about 1907 (University of Michigan Museum of Art; Smithsonian). Barber printed it in 1904; the dated museum examples run 1903 to 1906. The Kovels' 1903 to the present is the pottery's span, not the mark's.

sources.where: p. 34; photo Fig. 39, p. 35 (Albion College pieces)

disagreements: Order of marks: Pear and Evans put the maple-leaf mark after Perry/Revelation and before the round Pewabic seal; Catallo (pp. 33-34) puts it after the round mark and the PP mark.

Pear (p. 34) says the leaf mark carried the word Pewabic but also says the Pewabic name was adopted only in 1905; Barber printed the mark in 1904 and the Pewabic timeline and Catallo date the name to 1903.
Kovels date the mark 1903-present (the pottery's dates); every other source ends it about 1907.

entries.name: PEWABIC DETROIT round seal
entries.looks_like: A small circle about an inch across: PEWABIC round the top, DETROIT round the bottom, the middle plain or with a small dot. Often pressed twice, and often half filled with glaze.
entries.means: Pewabic's standard mark for most of Mary Chase Perry Stratton's career, and the commonest Pewabic mark.
entries.where_on_piece: base, usually in the trimmed centre of the foot
entries.date_note: Its start is given as 1903, about 1908 or about 1910; it was used until production stopped in 1969 (some sources say early 1967). Firmly dated pieces carry it from 1917 (bought by Freer) through the 1920s to 1950. Pear and Evans call it a Pewabic Pottery seal, but every example recorded on a piece reads PEWABIC DETROIT.

sources.where: p. 229, as given in Lehner (1988), Lehner p. 342
p. 343, mark no. 3 ('shown in various directories of the 1950's')

disagreements: Start: Pear p. 210 says Heerich stamped a new circular seal 'bearing the name "Pewabic Pottery"' in 1903; Catallo calls the circle the first Pewabic mark; the University of Michigan catalogue says from about 1910; Brunk's earliest examples are about 1908-1909; Evans (as Lehner gives him) puts the circular mark after the Revelation and maple-leaf marks.
Wording: Pear p. 210 and Evans (as Lehner gives him) call it a 'Pewabic Pottery' seal; every transcription on a real piece found reads PEWABIC / DETROIT.

End: 1969 (Day Books end; the University of Michigan catalogue). Pewabic and Catallo say Michigan State ended production pottery at the start of 1967. Freer's gallery label says Pewabic was made 'from 1903 until 1965'.
Size: Pear - about one inch; a Cranbrook record seen only as a search-engine snippet - 3/4 inch (not verified; Cranbrook's site blocked automated reading).

entries.name: PEWABIC DETROIT round paper label
entries.looks_like: A round tan paper sticker about an inch across, PEWABIC printed round the top and DETROIT round the bottom in black or thin dark letters, often with a price or number pencilled in the middle.
entries.means: Pewabic's sales label; Pear says many pieces were labeled instead of stamped.
entries.where_on_piece: base; one Cooper Hewitt vase has it inside the rim because glaze covered the base
entries.date_note: Brunk shows it on pieces of about 1903 and 1904; the University of Michigan says from about 1910. Used until 1969. Dated museum examples: 1908, 1912, 1917. A label can be put on later than the piece was made, and many have come off.
disagreements: Start: about 1903-1904 (Brunk 2007 examples; the Detroit Institute of Arts's 1908 example) versus about 1910 (the University of Michigan catalogue).

entries.name: M1, M2 and M3 labels
entries.looks_like: A small handwritten paper label reading M1, M2 or M3, or M1 pencilled under DETROIT on the round label, on the base of an exceptional piece.
entries.means: M for museum quality: pieces set aside as the best the pottery made.
entries.date_note: On pieces of about 1915 to 1925; no longer used by 1938. Pear says Charles Lang Freer chose and marked them; the University of Michigan says Mrs. Stratton made the labels at Freer's urging, which fits an M1 on a vase of 1924 and the M2 shown here, on a bottle the Detroit Institute of Arts dates 1920, both after Freer died in 1919.

sources.where: section 'M1, M2, and M3 Paper Labels'

disagreements: Who marked them: Pear says Charles L. Freer selected and marked the pieces; the University of Michigan catalogue (citing Ella Peters) says Freer encouraged Mrs. Stratton and she devised the labels.
Brunk 2007 shows an M1 label on a vase dated 1924, five years after Freer's death, which fits Stratton applying them.
The University of Michigan catalogue's author had seen only M1 and M2 and was told of M3; Pear and Brunk 2007 name M3.
Pear's 'The first two numbers represent the year' (caption, p. 201) refers to Freer Gallery accession numbers, not to the M labels or to marks on the pots.

entries.name: Charles Lang Freer's inventory numbers
entries.looks_like: Small rectangular white stickers with a dashed black border and a printed four-digit number, often two of them, or a number painted in orange inside the foot.
entries.means: Freer's own inventory numbers: the piece belonged to Charles Lang Freer, Pewabic's first great patron. Not a Pewabic mark.
entries.where_on_piece: base; painted numbers inside the foot
entries.date_note: Freer bought Pewabic from 1903 to 1918; his collection went to the Freer Gallery in 1920. The labels are identified as his by Brunk; the Freer Gallery records transcribe them without naming them.

sources.where: F1912.103; F1917.440 (stickers transcribed; the records do not say whose numbers they are)

disagreements: The identification as Freer's labels is Brunk's; the Freer Gallery's own records transcribe the stickers without naming them.

entries.name: WBS, William Buck Stratton
entries.looks_like: The letters WBS scratched or written on the base, usually with a year such as 1933 or 1935; once W B STRATTON in full.
entries.means: Designed or made by William Buck Stratton, the architect of the pottery building and Mary Chase Perry's husband.
entries.date_note: Dated examples run from October 1932 to 1935; pieces of 1927 are attributed to him. He died in 1938. Evans says WBS appears on early pieces, which the dated examples do not bear out.

sources.where: p. 229, as given in Lehner (1988), Lehner p. 342

disagreements: Evans (as Lehner gives him): 'early pieces'. Dated examples: 1932-1935.
The Detroit Institute of Arts F82.59 (1940-1945) is recorded as 'W B 5' painted in black. It may be a misreading of WBS, but Stratton died in 1938; unresolved.

entries.name: Modern Pewabic stamps
entries.looks_like: A small round seal on the base: PEWABIC round the top, DETROIT round the bottom, and the year in the middle, as on a vase of 1992 at The Henry Ford. Tiles carry a Pewabic stamp on the back.
entries.means: Made by today's nonprofit Pewabic Pottery, which restarted production in 1983.
entries.where_on_piece: base of vessels; back of tiles
entries.date_note: Pewabic's own pages mention its signature Pewabic, Detroit and artisan stamps. The one modern stamp found in a museum, on a vase of 1992 at The Henry Ford, is the round seal with the year in its middle; the old seal has none. Whether every modern piece carries a year, and since when, is not documented.
